content: The references provided are a collection of studies, reviews, and guidelines related to water, sanitation, hygiene (WASH), and their impacts on public health. 1. E. Arikpo et al. (2015): This study systematically reviewed the promotion of handwashing as a preventive measure against diarrheal diseases. It highlights the effectiveness of hand hygiene interventions in reducing the incidence of diarrhea, particularly in low-resource settings. 2. Fewtrell and Bartram (2001): This publication discusses water quality guidelines and standards, focusing on risk assessment and management for waterborne infectious diseases. It provides a comprehensive framework for ensuring safe water use and minimizing health risks. 3. Fotedar (2001): This research investigates the role of houseflies (Musca domestica) as vectors in the transmission of Vibrio cholerae in India. It emphasizes the importance of controlling fly populations to prevent cholera outbreaks. 4. Freeman et al. (2014): This systematic review examines global handwashing practices and their health effects. It underscores the critical role of hygiene in reducing disease transmission and improving health outcomes. 5. Freeman et al. (2017): This meta-analysis evaluates the impact of sanitation on infectious diseases and nutritional status. It provides evidence that improved sanitation significantly reduces disease burden and enhances nutritional health. 6. Fuller and Eisenberg (2016): This study explores the concept of herd protection achieved through interventions in drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene. It demonstrates how community-wide improvements can protect even those not directly involved in interventions. 7. Garn et al. (2017): This systematic review assesses the effects of sanitation interventions on latrine coverage and usage. It highlights the importance of sustained adoption and proper use of sanitation facilities. 8. Glas et al. (2001): This review focuses on the occupational health risks of hepatitis A among workers exposed to sewage. It emphasizes the need for protective measures in high-risk occupational settings. 9. Heijnen et al. (2014): This systematic review compares shared sanitation facilities with individual household latrines, analyzing their respective health outcomes. It identifies the limitations of shared facilities in ensuring optimal health benefits. 10. Heijnen et al. (2015): This cross-sectional study examines the use, accessibility, and cleanliness of neighbor-shared versus communal latrines in urban slums in Odisha, India. It provides insights into the challenges of sanitation in densely populated areas. 11. Hulland et al. (2015): This literature review identifies factors influencing the sustained adoption of safe water, hygiene, and sanitation technologies. It highlights the importance of behavioral, social, and environmental factors in achieving long-term success. 12. Ingalinella et al. (2002): This publication addresses the challenges of fecal sludge management in urban areas, proposing strategies, regulations, and treatment options to improve sanitation systems. 13. Jeggli et al. (2004): This study investigates the prevalence of hepatitis E, Helicobacter pylori, and gastrointestinal symptoms among wastewater workers, emphasizing occupational health risks. 14. Khin et al. (1989): This research examines the carriage of enteric bacterial pathogens by houseflies in Yangon, Myanmar, highlighting their role in disease transmission. 15. Kiendrebeogo (2012): This study explores the relationship between access to improved water sources and rural productivity, providing cross-country evidence of the economic benefits of safe water access. 16. Knight and Presnell (2005): This case report discusses fatalities caused by sewer gas exposure, reviewing the associated health risks and preventive measures. 17. Lanata et al. (1998): This study reflects on the sources of diarrheal pathogens in a Peruvian shantytown, emphasizing the importance of addressing fecal contamination in public health interventions. 18. Lin et al. (2013): This analysis identifies volatile compounds emitted from latrines, providing insights into odor management and environmental impacts of sanitation systems. 19. Majorin et al. (2018): This Cochrane review evaluates interventions aimed at improving the disposal of child feces to prevent diarrhea and soil-transmitted helminth infections. 20. Majorin et al. (2017): This study identifies potential exposure sources along the child feces management pathway in urban slums in Odisha, India, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. 21. Miller-Petrie et al. (2016): This research focuses on infant and young child feces management in Cambodia, analyzing enabling products for hygienic collection, transport, and disposal. 22. Mills et al. (2018): This study proposes an approach to assess fecal pathogen flows and public health risks in urban environments, informing sanitation planning. 23. Morita et al. (2016): This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness of safe child feces disposal interventions, providing evidence for their role in reducing disease transmission. 24. Nakagiri et al. (2016): This review examines the performance of pit latrines in urban areas of Sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on usage, filling rates, insect presence, and odor nuisances. 25. Novotný et al. (2017): This systematic review identifies contextual factors and motivations affecting rural community sanitation in lowand middle-income countries. 26. Oswald et al. (2017): This study investigates the relationship between active trachoma and community sanitation use in Ethiopia, highlighting the importance of sanitation in trachoma control. 27. Overbo et al. (2016): This systematic review examines the influence of programming and enabling environments on sanitation adoption and sustained use. 28. Padhi et al. (2015): This prospective cohort study in rural India links poor sanitation practices to adverse pregnancy outcomes, emphasizing the need for improved sanitation for maternal health. 29. Rand et al. (2015): This research brief reviews current child feces disposal practices, identifying gaps and opportunities for improvement. 30. Rehfuess et al. (2009): This publication discusses health sector functions to secure environmental health, emphasizing cost-effective interventions. 31. Rheinländer et al. (2015): This study redefines shared sanitation, exploring its implications for public health and community well-being. 32. Routray et al. (2015): This qualitative study explores socio-cultural and behavioral factors constraining latrine adoption in rural coastal Odisha, India. 33. Sclar et al. (2016): This systematic review assesses the impact of sanitation on indicators of fecal exposure along principal transmission pathways. 34. Sclar et al. (2017): This review examines the effects of sanitation on cognitive development and school absence, highlighting its broader societal impacts. 35. Sclar et al. (2018): This study explores the relationship between sanitation and mental and social well-being, providing a qualitative synthesis of evidence. 36. Speich et al. (2016): This meta-analysis evaluates the effect of sanitation and water treatment on intestinal protozoa infections, providing evidence for their health benefits. 37. Strande et al. (2014): This publication outlines a systems approach for implementing and operating fecal sludge management, emphasizing its importance in urban sanitation. 38. Sultana et al. (2013): This study introduces an improved tool for household feces management in rural Bangladeshi communities. 39. Szostakowska et al. (2004): This research identifies Cryptosporidium parvum and Giardia lamblia recovered from flies on cattle farms and landfills, highlighting their role in pathogen transmission. 40. Thorn and Kerekes (2001): This literature survey reviews health effects among employees in sewage treatment plants, emphasizing occupational health risks. 41. Thye et al. (2011): This critical review evaluates technologies for pit latrine emptying in developing countries, identifying challenges and opportunities for improvement. 42. Tiwari (2008): This study reviews occupational health hazards faced by sewage and sanitary workers, emphasizing the need for protective measures. 43. UNICEF (2012): This report focuses on water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in schools, highlighting its importance for child health and education. 44. United Nations (2015): This resolution recognizes the human rights to safe drinking water and sanitation, emphasizing their role in achieving sustainable development. 45. Venkataramanan et al. (2018): This systematic review evaluates the evidence and quality of community-led total sanitation interventions, providing insights into their effectiveness. 46. WSSCC and UN Women (2014): This report examines menstrual hygiene management practices in Senegal, emphasizing the need for gender-sensitive sanitation solutions. 47. WaterAid (2016): This synthesis report provides insights for planning urban sanitation in Ghana, India, and the Philippines, emphasizing clean city initiatives. 48. WHO (2006): These guidelines address the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater, providing a comprehensive framework for policy and regulatory aspects. 49. WHO (2008): This document outlines essential environmental health standards in healthcare, emphasizing the importance of WASH in health facilities. 50. WHO (2011): These guidelines for drinking-water quality provide a global standard for ensuring safe water access. 51. WHO (2016): This publication outlines core components of infection prevention and control programs at national and healthcare facility levels. 52. WHO and UNICEF (2018): This practical guide, WASH FIT, aims to improve the quality of care in healthcare facilities through water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions. 53. Yates et al. (2015): This systematic review examines the impact of WASH interventions on the health and well-being of people living with HIV, highlighting their critical role in improving quality of life.
